title: System Properties
description: Classify systems as linear, time-invariant, causal, memoryless, invertible and stable.

study.title: Linearity
study.body: A system is **linear** if it obeys superposition: if $x_1 \to y_1$ and $x_2 \to y_2$, then scaled and added inputs give the same combination of outputs. Quick checks: zero input must give zero output, and doubling the input must double the output. $y = 2x(t) + 3$ fails (offset), $y = x^2(t)$ fails (doubling gives ×4), but $y = t\,x(t)$ and $y = x(t-1)$ are linear.
study.formula: a x_1 + b x_2 \;\to\; a y_1 + b y_2

study.title: Time invariance
study.body: A system is **time-invariant** if delaying the input just delays the output. Test: feed $x(t - t_0)$ and compare with $y(t - t_0)$. Red flags for time variance: an explicit $t$ outside the argument of $x$ (like $t\,x(t)$ or $\cos(t)\,x(t)$), and time scaling or reversal ($x(2t)$, $x(-t)$).
study.formula: x(t - t_0) \to y(t - t_0) \quad \text{for every } t_0

study.title: Memory and causality
study.body:
**Memoryless:** $y(t)$ depends only on $x$ at the same instant ($y = 3x^2(t)$). **Causal:** $y(t)$ depends only on present and past inputs. $x(t+1)$ is non-causal.
**Pitfall:** $y(t) = x(t/2)$ is non-causal, because at $t = -2$ it needs $x(-1)$, a future value. Every memoryless system is causal.

study.title: BIBO stability
study.body: A system is **BIBO stable** if every bounded input ($|x| \le M$) gives a bounded output. The integrator fails: a step input gives a ramp. $y = t\,x(t)$ fails too. An LTI system is stable exactly when its impulse response is absolutely integrable:

study.title: Invertibility
study.body: A system is **invertible** if different inputs always give different outputs, so the input can be recovered. $y = x(t - 2)$ (inverse: advance by 2) and $y = 3x + 1$ (inverse: $(y-1)/3$) are invertible. $y = x^2$ loses the sign and $y = dx/dt$ loses constants, so they are not.

study.title: Worked example: a modulator
study.body:
$y(t) = x(t)\cos(\omega_0 t)$:
- **Linear:** $(ax_1 + bx_2)\cos = a y_1 + b y_2$.
- **Time-varying:** a delayed input gives $x(t-t_0)\cos(\omega_0 t) \ne y(t - t_0)$.
- **Memoryless and causal:** uses only $x(t)$.
- **Stable:** $|y| \le |x|$.
- **Not invertible:** $x$ is lost wherever $\cos(\omega_0 t) = 0$.

steps.title: Systems and linearity
steps.body: A system maps an input signal $x(t)$ to an output $y(t)$. It is **linear** when superposition holds: the response to $a x_1 + b x_2$ is $a y_1 + b y_2$. Two quick tests: zero in must give zero out, and doubling the input must double the output.

steps.explanation: $t\,[a x_1 + b x_2] = a\,t x_1 + b\,t x_2$: superposition holds (the factor $t$ makes it time-varying, not nonlinear). $3x+2$ gives 2 for zero input; $x^2$ and $|x|$ do not scale: doubling $x$ quadruples $x^2$, and $|-x| \ne -|x|$.

steps.title: Time invariance
steps.body: A system is **time-invariant** if a delayed input produces the same output, just delayed. To test: apply $x(t - t_0)$, compute the output, and compare it with $y(t - t_0)$. An explicit $t$ multiplying the signal, or a scaled time argument like $x(2t)$, usually breaks it.
steps.formula: x(t) \to y(t) \;\Rightarrow\; x(t - t_0) \to y(t - t_0)

steps.explanation: Delay the input: $x_1(t) = x(t - t_0)$ gives $y_1(t) = x_1(2t) = x(2t - t_0)$. But the delayed output is $y(t - t_0) = x(2t - 2t_0)$. They differ, so the compressor is **time-varying**.

steps.title: Memory and causality
steps.body: A **memoryless** system uses only the present input value: $y(t) = f(x(t))$. A **causal** system may use present and past inputs, but never future ones; every physical real-time system is causal.
steps.formula: y(t_1) \text{ depends only on } x(t),\ t \le t_1

steps.explanation: $x(t) + x(t-1)$ uses the present and one second ago. $x(t+1)$ needs the future. $x(-t)$ at $t = -1$ needs $x(1)$, which is future. $x(2t)$ at $t = 1$ needs $x(2)$, also future.

steps.title: Stability and invertibility
steps.body: **BIBO stable:** every bounded input gives a bounded output. An integrator is not: a constant input produces an ever-growing ramp. **Invertible:** the input can always be recovered from the output; $y = x^2$ is not invertible because $x$ and $-x$ give the same output.

steps.prompt: Each system has exactly one of these four properties missing: linearity, time invariance, causality, stability. Match each to the one it lacks.
steps.explanation:
- Integrator: linear, time-invariant, causal, but a step input gives an unbounded ramp.
- $x(t+1)$: an LTI advance, stable, but it uses the future.
- $\cos(t)x(t)$: linear, causal, $|y| \le |x|$, but the gain changes with time.
- $x^2$: time-invariant, causal, stable for bounded $x$, but not linear.

With $x = 0$ the output is 1, not 0. Superposition fails: $x_1 + x_2$ gives $x_1 + x_2 + 1$, while $y_1 + y_2 = x_1 + x_2 + 2$. Such a system is called **incrementally linear** (linear plus an offset).

Linear: $(a x_1 + b x_2)\cos(100t) = a y_1 + b y_2$. Time-varying: the input $x(t - t_0)$ gives $x(t - t_0)\cos(100t)$, but $y(t - t_0) = x(t - t_0)\cos(100(t - t_0))$. The carrier does not shift with the input.

It is a sum of shifted inputs with constant coefficients, so it is linear and time-invariant. $y[n]$ needs $x[n+1]$, one sample in the future, so it is non-causal. (The backward difference $x[n] - x[n-1]$ would be causal.)

steps.prompt: A linear system gives $y_1({{t0}}) = {{p}}$ for input $x_1$ and $y_2({{t0}}) = {{q}}$ for input $x_2$. Find the output at $t = {{t0}}$ for input $x(t) = {{a}}x_1(t) - {{b}}x_2(t)$.
steps.explanation: Superposition: $y = {{a}}y_1 - {{b}}y_2$, so $y({{t0}}) = {{a}}\cdot({{p}}) - {{b}}\cdot({{q}})$ = {{a*p-b*q}}. Linearity alone is enough here, since both inputs go into the same system at the same time.

steps.prompt: An LTI system responds to $x(t)$ with $y(t) = {{A}}\left(1 - e^{-t/{{tau}}}\right)u(t)$ ($t$ in s). Find the output at $t = {{t0}}$ s when the input is ${{K}}\,x(t - {{T}})$.
steps.explanation: Time invariance: the delay carries over, so the output is ${{K}}\,y(t - {{T}})$ (linearity gives the factor {{K}}). At $t = {{t0}}$: ${{K}}\cdot{{A}}\left(1 - e^{-({{t0}} - {{T}})/{{tau}}}\right)$ = {{K*A*(1-exp(-(t0-T)/tau))}}.
For $t > 0$, $t/2 < t$, so it looks into the past. But for negative times, e.g. $t = -4$, it needs $x(-2)$, which lies in the **future**. A system must be causal for all $t$, so this one is not.

steps.prompt: An LTI system has $h(t) = {{K}}e^{-{{a}}t}u(t)$. The input is bounded by $|x(t)| \le {{M}}$. Find the guaranteed upper bound on $|y(t)|$ from $|y| \le M\int|h|\,dt$.
steps.explanation: $|y(t)| = \left|\int h(\tau)x(t - \tau)d\tau\right| \le M\int_0^\infty {{K}}e^{-{{a}}\tau}d\tau = M\frac{K}{a} = {{M}}\cdot\frac{ {{K}} }{ {{a}} }$ = {{M*K/a}}. Since $\int|h| = {{K/a}}$ is finite, the system is BIBO stable.
$x^2$ maps $x$ and $-x$ to the same output, so the sign is lost. $x^3$ is one-to-one (inverse: cube root), a delay is undone by an advance, and $4x+1$ is undone by $(y - 1)/4$.
Memoryless means $y(t)$ uses only $x(t)$ at the same instant. That is never a future value, so the system is automatically causal. The converse is false: a delay $x(t - 1)$ is causal but has memory.

options: linear, time-varying, with memory and stable
steps.explanation: Linear: $n(a x_1 + b x_2) = a y_1 + b y_2$. Time-varying: the gain $n$ changes with time. Memoryless: only $x[n]$ is used. Unstable: the bounded input $x[n] = 1$ gives $y[n] = n$, which grows without limit.

- Linear: the integral of $a x_1 + b x_2$ is $a y_1 + b y_2$.
- Time-varying: $x(t - t_0)$ gives $\int_{-\infty}^{2t - t_0}x$, but $y(t - t_0) = \int_{-\infty}^{2t - 2t_0}x$.
- Non-causal: for $t>0$ it integrates up to $2t > t$.
- Unstable: a step gives an unbounded ramp.
Doubling $x$ quadruples $y$, so it is not linear. It is time-invariant (both factors shift together), causal (present and past only) and stable ($|y| \le M^2$). It does have memory, through $x(t-1)$.

steps.prompt: An LTI system with impulse response $h(t) = u(t)$ is BIBO stable.
steps.explanation: $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|u(t)|dt = \int_0^\infty 1\,dt = \infty$. This $h$ is the integrator: the bounded input $u(t)$ gives the unbounded output $r(t) = t\,u(t)$.

steps.prompt: Order the steps to test whether a system is time-invariant.
items: Find the output $y(t)$ for a general input $x(t)$
Apply the delayed input $x(t - t_0)$ and compute its output $y_1(t)$
Delay the original output to get $y(t - t_0)$
Compare: if $y_1(t) = y(t - t_0)$ for every $x$ and $t_0$, it is time-invariant
steps.explanation: Two outputs are compared: the response to the shifted input, and the shifted response. Be careful in the first: replace $x(\cdot)$ by $x(\cdot - t_0)$ **only inside $x$**, not every $t$ in the formula.

Linear: $a x_1[2n] + b x_2[2n] = a y_1 + b y_2$. Time-varying: delaying the input by 1 gives $x[2n - 1]$, which picks the **odd** samples, while $y[n - 1] = x[2n - 2]$ picks the even ones. No shift of $y$ can produce the odd samples.

steps.prompt: A sensor amplifier gives {{m+c}} V out for 1 V in and {{3*m+c}} V out for 3 V in. Assuming $y = a x + b$, find the output for {{x0}} V in.
steps.explanation: Slope $a = \frac{ {{3*m+c}} - {{m+c}} }{3 - 1}$ = {{m}}, offset $b = {{m+c}} - {{m}}$ = {{c}} V. Output: ${{m}}\cdot{{x0}} + {{c}}$ = {{m*x0+c}} V. Scaling the 1 V result by {{x0}} (giving {{(m+c)*x0}} V) would be wrong: with the offset the system is not linear, only incrementally linear.

steps.prompt: An LTI system has step response $s(t) = \left(1 - e^{-t/{{tau}}}\right)u(t)$ ($t$ in s). The input is a pulse ${{A}}\left[u(t) - u(t - {{T}})\right]$. Find the output at $t = {{t0}}$ s.
steps.explanation: Linearity and time invariance: the pulse is ${{A}}u(t) - {{A}}u(t - {{T}})$, so $y(t) = {{A}}\left[s(t) - s(t - {{T}})\right]$. At $t = {{t0}}$: ${{A}}\left[(1 - e^{-{{t0}}/{{tau}}}) - (1 - e^{-{{t0-T}}/{{tau}}})\right]$ = {{A*((1-exp(-t0/tau)) - (1-exp(-(t0-T)/tau)))}}.
Whatever the input, $|\sin(\cdot)| \le 1$, so the output is always bounded by 1. (It is nonlinear, memoryless and time-invariant.)
